title: Fewest Copies to Contain a String
statement:
You get two strings, a and b. Write a out k times in a row (for k = 2, "xyz" becomes "xyzxyz").

Return the smallest k ≥ 1 for which b appears as a contiguous substring of the result, or -1 if no number of copies works.

examples.why: "xyzxyzxyz" contains it: b starts at the last letter of the first copy and ends inside the third. Two copies are only 6 letters and do not.
b already fits in a single copy, even though it is shorter than a.
In any number of copies, a is always followed by b. Adding copies never helps.

constraints: a and b consist of lowercase English letters
hints: If b fits somewhere in the copies, where can it start? Does it ever need to start after the end of the first copy?
No. Any match can be shifted back by whole copies of a, so it can start inside the first copy. Then k is at most ceil(b.length / a.length) + 1.
Build that many copies and look for b. The match position tells you how many copies were actually needed. A linear-time matcher such as KMP keeps the search O(n + m).

explain.intuition:
The repeated text is periodic, so if b occurs anywhere, it also occurs starting inside the first copy of a: just shift it back by whole copies. A match starting at index s < |a| ends at s + |b|, so it needs ceil((s + |b|) / |a|) copies, which is at most ceil(|b| / |a|) + 1.

That means you only ever need to check one text: a repeated ceil(|b| / |a|) + 1 times. Find the first occurrence of b there. If there is none, more copies would not create one, so the answer is -1.
steps: Let q = ceil(|b| / |a|) + 1 and build text = a repeated q times.
Find the first index s where b occurs in text (KMP gives O(n + m)).
If there is no match, return -1.
pitfalls: Stopping at ceil(|b| / |a|) copies. A match that starts late in a copy needs one more, as in the first example.
Looping "add another copy until it matches" with no upper limit. When the answer is -1 it never ends.
Assuming the answer is at least 1 only when b is longer than a. A short b inside a single copy gives 1.

solutions.title: Grow until long enough, then check one more
solutions.idea: Add copies until the text is at least as long as b. Check it, then check with one extra copy.
solutions.time: O((|a| + |b|) · |b|) worst case for a plain substring search

solutions.title: KMP on the bounded text
solutions.idea: Build the failure table for b, scan a repeated ceil(|b|/|a|) + 1 times once, and turn the first match position into a copy count.

followups: Solve it with a rolling hash (Rabin–Karp) instead of KMP. What do you do on a hash collision?
Return the smallest number of copies of a needed so that b is a subsequence, not a substring.
